The Loeb editor notes that Aulus Gellius says he was older than Socrates, which would put his birth before 470 BC.

preferred.display: About 370 BC (traditions give ages of 85, 90, 104 or 109)

alternatives.note: Roster year; it follows the tradition that he lived about 90 years.
Two medical reviews give 460 to 377 BC.
The Suda says he died at about 104.

historical_timeline.summary: Born on the island of Cos (Kos), of the Asclepiad guild of physicians, by the late ancient lives.

date.display: Late fifth or early fourth century BC

historical_timeline.summary: Named by Plato as a physician of Cos who taught medicine for a fee; later called 'the Great Hippocrates' by Aristotle. The writings that bear his name are by many authors.

date.display: About 370 BC (traditions give ages from 85 to 109)

historical_timeline.summary: Dies in Thessaly and is buried at Larissa, by the Suda; the year and his age are uncertain.

claims.statement: Plato names him in the Protagoras as 'Hippocrates of Cos, the Asclepiad', a physician who took pupils for a fee, and in the Phaedrus cites his method; Aristotle calls him 'the Great Hippocrates'. These are the earliest witnesses to him.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented core of his life: a physician and teacher of medicine from Cos. It anchors his work in the modern social history.

source_links.locator: thought of going to Hippocrates of Cos, the Asclepiad, and were about to give him your money
Hippocrates was a Coan, an Asclepiad, and a professional trainer of medical students; From Aristotle we learn that Hippocrates was already known as the Great Hippocrates

claims.statement: The three ancient lives (by Soranus, a late writer, and in the Suda and Tzetzes, all written many centuries after him) say that he was born on Cos in 460 BC, that his father Heraclides was a physician of the Asclepiad guild and taught him, and that he travelled widely in Greece; the Loeb editor finds 'a certain amount of fable' in them but nothing improbable in their broad outline.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Birth on Cos about 460 BC is accepted by modern scholars; the details of the lives are late and partly legendary.

source_links.locator: We possess three ancient biographies of Hippocrates: one by Suidas, one by Tzetzes, and one by Soranus, a late writer of uncertain date; born in Cos in 460 B.C.; In these accounts there is a certain amount of fable
Hippocrates of Cos was the son of Heraclides; He first studied under his father

claims.statement: How long he lived is not known: the traditions make him live 85, 90, 104 or 109 years, and the Suda says about 104. Some stories in the lives are legend; the Loeb editor notes that the tale of his staying the plague at Athens contradicts Thucydides.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The length of his life rests on late and conflicting traditions; the modern episode follows the ninety-year tradition only to place the index age and makes no claim about his real age at death.

source_links.locator: his life was a long one but of uncertain length, the traditions making him live 85, 90, 104 or 109 years; except the staying of the Athenian plague, which is directly contrary to the testimony of Thucydides
He lived a long life and died at about 104 years old

claims.statement: According to the Suda he died in Thessaly and was buried at Larissa.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the assumed setting of the modern episode; the date of his death is not known.

source_links.locator: He died in Thessaly and was buried at Larissa

claims.statement: The Hippocratic Corpus is not the work of one man. The Loeb editor describes it as the remains of a library of works 'of various dates and of different schools', a great part of which is 'neither by Hippocrates himself nor by his school'; Aristotle ascribed one of its treatises to Polybus, and Hippocrates is 'a name without writings'. Which treatises, if any, he wrote is still debated.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded so that no statement in the Corpus is attributed to him as fact.

source_links.locator: valuable works, of various dates and of different schools; a great part of its contents is neither by Hippocrates himself nor by his school; a name without writings, as Wilamowitz says; he assigns as the author not Hippocrates but Polybus

claims.statement: Modern medicine regards him as its founder: reviews call him 'the father of modern medicine' and 'the founding father of clinical medicine', for medicine based on observation of clinical signs rather than on religious or magical beliefs.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His reputation; it anchors the teaching theme of a physician as patient.

source_links.locator: Hippocrates of Kos (460-377 Before Common Era, BCE) is universally recognized as the father of modern medicine, which is based on observation of clinical signs
born on the Aegean island of Kos during the fifth century; the founding father of clinical medicine

claims.statement: Nothing about his own health is documented in the sources read: no illness, injury or cause of death is recorded. The roster's 'longevity; natural aging' is a lead only, resting on the disputed traditions of his age.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The thin chart is the point: the modern episode is built around normal aging, not a historical diagnosis.

source_links.locator: Such is the ancient account of Hippocrates, a name without writings
roster: own health largely undocumented; longevity; natural aging

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Healthy aging in a nonagenarian, with care built on function rather than disease: an 89-year-old physician who still teaches comes in after a wellness screening notes slower walking and a near-fall. The episode covers the comprehensive geriatric assessment (gait speed, Timed Up and Go, chair stands and the four-stage balance test, grip strength, MoCA and Mini-Cog, GDS-15, hearing and vision, nutrition and continence) and frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale and the FRAIL scale, ICFSR 2019); the Age-Friendly Health Systems 4Ms (What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility); a deprescribing review with the AGS Beers Criteria 2023 (over-the-counter naproxen and diphenhydramine stopped); knee osteoarthritis diagnosed clinically without imaging and treated with exercise, topical diclofenac and acetaminophen (ACR/AF 2019); falls prevention by STEADI and the World Falls Guidelines, with a strength and balance program; bone health in an older man (DXA, FRAX and vitamin D); a sick visit for a cold that tests the deprescribing plan; vaccinations for his age (pneumococcal, RSV, recombinant zoster, high-dose influenza); and advance care planning centered on what matters most to him.

documentation.chief_complaint: Two-week review, seen the same day by geriatric medicine

hpi.narrative: Hippocrates stopped the naproxen and the diphenhydramine after intake. For the first three nights he slept poorly; since then he has slept about six hours with a fixed bedtime, no afternoon wine and a short walk after supper. He takes acetaminophen once or twice a day, and the knee pain on his stairs is 4 of 10. He has had no falls and holds the rail. His vitamin B12 was drawn this morning. He sees Dr. Lindqvist-Bamba of geriatric medicine this afternoon. He asks plainly whether his slower walking is age or something that can be treated.

referral.question: Slower walking, knee pain on stairs and one near-fall in an independent 89-year-old physician who still teaches, with a gait speed of 0.78 m/s, a Timed Up and Go of 13.8 seconds and low grip strength on comprehensive geriatric assessment. Please advise on the cause, frailty, his medicines, falls prevention and bone health, in a plan built on what matters most to him
referral.pertinent_history: His annual wellness screening at his previous practice noted that he walks more slowly. Over six months the hill into town for his teaching has become harder, his knees hurt on his stairs (5 of 10) with ten minutes of morning stiffness, and one night he nearly fell on the stairs and caught the rail. No dizziness, blackouts, numbness or weight loss. Over-the-counter naproxen 220 to 440 mg most days for about two years and diphenhydramine 25 mg three or four nights a week for sleep, both stopped today; acetaminophen as needed and vitamin D3 started. Never smoked; one small cup of watered wine with dinner. Lives alone in his own house with stairs; a neighbor looks in daily; independent in all daily and instrumental activities. Assessment today: gait speed 0.78 m/s; Timed Up and Go 13.8 seconds; 7 chair stands in 30 seconds; tandem stance held 6 seconds; grip 24 kg right and 22 kg left; MoCA 26; GDS-15 2; whispered voice heard both ears; reads with glasses; MNA-SF 12 (normal); up once at night to pass urine, no leakage; Clinical Frailty Scale 3; FRAIL 1 of 5. Blood pressure 138/74 seated without an orthostatic fall; BMI 22.7. Results: eGFR 63, calcium 9.3 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, TSH 2.1, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 24 ng/mL. No known allergy. What matters most to him: to keep walking into town to teach and to manage his stairs at home.
questions: What is causing the slower gait and the near-fall, and is there anything to treat beyond the knees?
Do you agree with stopping naproxen and diphenhydramine, and what should replace them?
Is he frail, and what exercise or rehabilitation do you advise?
What falls prevention does he need under STEADI?
How should his bone health be assessed and managed?

consultant_note.history: Thank you for asking me to see Hippocrates, an 89-year-old physician who still teaches two mornings a week, for slower walking and a near-fall. The history is as in your letter. He describes knee pain on stairs and on the hill, worse at the end of the day, with brief morning stiffness, and a sense that his thighs tire before his breath does. The near-fall was at night on the stairs, on a night he had taken diphenhydramine. He has had no dizziness on standing, blackouts, vertigo, numbness, tremor or change in memory. In the two weeks since stopping naproxen and diphenhydramine he sleeps about six hours with a sleep routine, and the knees are 4 of 10 on acetaminophen. He told me what matters most: to walk into town to teach, and to stay in his own house.
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Your comprehensive geriatric assessment: gait speed 0.78 m/s, Timed Up and Go 13.8 seconds, 7 chair stands, tandem stance 6 seconds, grip 24 and 22 kg, MoCA 26, GDS-15 2, Clinical Frailty Scale 3, FRAIL 1 of 5. assessment.assessment: Knee osteoarthritis by the ACR clinical criteria; no X-ray is needed for the diagnosis. With quadriceps weakness and reduced balance it is the main cause of his slower gait. Diphenhydramine at night added to the risk on the night of the near-fall. I found no orthostatic, neurologic, thyroid, B12 or visual cause.
Naproxen (chronic NSAID use at 89, with an eGFR of 63) and diphenhydramine (strongly anticholinergic) are both on the Beers list; stopping them was right.

Pre-frail (Clinical Frailty Scale 3, FRAIL 1 of 5) with low grip strength; at increased risk of falls by STEADI because of the near-fall, the slow Timed Up and Go and the short tandem stance. Both are likely to improve with exercise.
A man of 89 at risk of falls, with vitamin D insufficiency; his fracture risk should be measured.

recommendations: Treat the knees as the cause of the slower gait: exercise first, diclofenac 1% gel to each painful knee up to four times a day, and acetaminophen as needed within 3,000 mg a day; no X-ray unless the picture changes (question 1)
Keep naproxen and diphenhydramine stopped; replace the sleep aid with a fixed sleep routine and no sleep medicine; check every over-the-counter purchase with the clinic or pharmacist (question 2)

Twelve weeks of physical therapy with a progressive strength and balance program based on Otago, then tai chi twice a week; repeat gait speed, Timed Up and Go, chair stands, balance and grip after the program (question 3)

Falls prevention under STEADI: a home safety check by the physical therapist, a second stair rail and night lights, shoes with a back indoors, and a yearly eye examination; continue vitamin D3 (question 4)

DXA of the spine and hips with FRAX; treat with an osteoporosis medicine only if FRAX reaches the BHOF thresholds or there is osteoporosis or a fragility fracture; vitamin D3 1,000 units daily with a recheck after about three months, and calcium from food (question 5)
Keep the plan anchored on what matters most to him (4Ms), and offer advance care planning at his wellness visit

consultant_note.follow_up: Geriatric medicine review in a year, or sooner after any fall or if the program does not help; primary care to repeat the mobility measures after the program.
